How LDLib draws the text in its own interfaces. Does not affect vanilla screens or other mods.

Vanilla hands text to Minecraft untouched. SDF samples one scalable atlas: smooth at any size or angle, a little soft up close. Raster redraws each glyph at the size it appears at: sharpest, but a separate atlas per size. Auto uses raster for still text on the pixel grid and SDF for anything scaled, rotated or animated.
Edge length in pixels of one glyph atlas page. Larger pages fit more glyphs, so a screen full of text costs fewer draw calls.
Pixel height one em is rasterized at when building the distance field. Higher keeps sharp corners sharper at large text sizes, at the cost of atlas space.
Multiplier on the width of the anti aliased edge. Above 1 is crisper, below 1 is softer.
Thickens or thins strokes by a fraction of a pixel. Raise slightly if small text looks too thin.
Largest text size, in device pixels, that will be rasterized at its drawn size. Anything larger uses the distance field instead. A text element's size works out to font size times GUI scale.
Seconds a rasterized size may go undrawn before its atlas is freed. Keeps zooming through many sizes from using memory without bound.
Reuse where each glyph goes between frames instead of working it out again every frame. Turn off only if text ever renders with the wrong styling.

A Generator consists of two main parts
The Stator, built out of Coils strung on Shafts (and optionally Housings)
This part generates a magnetic field, through a process called Excitation
As well as the Armature, built out of Rotors, a Commutator, and a Clutch
This is where electricity is generated. In typical setups, electrical load should be connected to the commutator.
To start generating electricity you must provide an Excitation Current to the Stator, through a Device Connector
Now lets crank up the voltage!
At this point you might have thought of a small problem.
2.Resistance - The 'excitation loop resistance' must be low enough to allow for the field to build up, but not too low as to not overpower the coils.
3.Rotation speed - The generator must spin fast enough to generate enough of the initial starting current and build up the field.
How do you provide excitation current if you have no other power source?
This is where the concept of Self-Excitation comes into play.
The stator coils posses a small residual magnetic field which can be used to start a feedback reaction.
To have better control of the output voltage, we'll use a Rheostat.
A self-excited generator is sensitive to a couple of factors.
1.Rotation direction - The generator will only work when spinning one way, stator wiring must be flipped for it to work the other way.
Generator voltage will drop when a load is connected
This effect can be reduced by utilizing the Carbon Pile Regulator

There are some blocks that let light through like glass, water, leaves and a few other blocks.
A Solar Panels output is based on an IV curve, Google "Solar Panel IV curve" for an image of a general IV curve.
There are a few terms you need to know.
Voc is the max voltage of the Solar Panel with no load on it.
Isc is the short current of the Solar Panel aka the current you would get placing a wire between the positive and negative.
Vmp and Imp are the points along the IV curve where the Solar Panel makes the most power, these points shift around depending on the environmental conditions of the Solar Panel.
A simple way to use a Solar Panel is by impedance matching it to your load.
For example if a Solar Panels Vmp is 21.2V and Imp is 7.8A, Ohm's law dictates that the optimal load resistance would be 2.71 Ohms.
The further you get from that resistance the less overall power the panel will make.

If enabled, only the faces of blocks which are facing the camera will be submitted for rendering. This can eliminate a large number of block faces very early in the rendering process, which greatly improves rendering performance. Some resource packs may have issues with this option, so try disabling it if you're seeing holes in blocks.

If enabled, chunks which are determined to be fully hidden by fog effects will not be rendered, helping to improve performance. The improvement can be more dramatic when fog effects are heavier (such as while underwater), but it may cause undesirable visual artifacts between the sky and fog in some scenarios.

If enabled, entities which are within the camera viewport, but not inside of a visible chunk, will be skipped during rendering. This optimization uses the visibility data which already exists for chunk rendering and does not add overhead.

If enabled, only the animated textures which are determined to be visible in the current image will be updated. This can provide a significant performance improvement on some hardware, especially with heavier resource packs. If you experience issues with some textures not being animated, try disabling this option.
For debugging only. Specifies the maximum number of frames which can be in-flight to the GPU. Changing this value is not recommended, as very low or high values may create frame rate instability.

For debugging only. If enabled, persistent memory mappings will be used for the staging buffer so that unnecessary memory copies can be avoided. Disabling this can be useful for narrowing down the cause of graphical corruption.\n\nRequires OpenGL 4.4 or ARB_buffer_storage.

Specifies the number of threads to use for chunk building and sorting. Using more threads can speed up chunk loading and update speed, but may negatively impact frame times. The default value is usually good enough for all situations.

If set to "Deferred", rendering will never wait for nearby chunk updates to finish, even if they are important. This can greatly improve frame rates in some scenarios, but it may create significant visual lag where blocks take a while to appear or disappear. "Immediate" eliminates visual lag by blocking the frame until chunk updates are complete while "Soon" allows at most one frame of visual lag.

Determines what approach is used to make translucent blocks (not entities or items) look correct even when they intersect or have unusual shapes, such as waterlogged stained glass panes. "Basic" disables this feature and such blocks may render incorrectly. "Safe" limits the amount of newly generated geometry to prevent instability in extreme cases, while "Unlimited" imposes no limit.

Controls how the translucent geometry of entities is sorted. "Enhanced" sorts by the closest point to the camera, which improves rendering accuracy for translucent quads with different sizes, at a small CPU cost. "Default" uses the standard sorting.
When enabled, the OpenGL context will be created with error checking disabled. This slightly improves rendering performance, but it can make debugging sudden unexplained crashes much harder.
